notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa036.opp-la: Scanning errors corrected silently where evident (e.g. 'PIUMUM' for PRIMUM, 'crededirat' for crediderat, 'iugem' for lugent, 'otero' for utero, 'ulero' for ultro). The section numbers '305', '308', '307', '309' are page numbers of the printed edition and are omitted; the canon-law reference '(32, q. 5, c. Revera)' is an editorial citation and is omitted. Line ref .20 contains both §14 and §15 in the source. In §4 the quotation combines Lam. 1:12 and 1:18. In §16 'iugem' read as 'lugent' (they mourn). In §12 'paradisi' rendered 'garden' as in the Susanna story.

Section numbers corrected from scanning errors (25→23, 50→30, 27hO→27. O). 'Elam' read as Evam (Eve). In 26 the quotation 'you have acted in secret…' is 2 Samuel 12:12 (II Reg. in the Vulgate numbering). 'scecuturium nuptiurum' read as saecularium nuptiarum. Section 19 'spiritu' rendered 'breath' (life).

Section numbers are misprinted by the scan; they are given here in sequence as 32 and 33 where the text reads '52' and '35', and 41 for '4i'. Section 34: 'pro illa nece quae facta dicitur in occulto' alludes to a killing (presumably of a child) said to have been done secretly. Section 32: 'depopulatione' is odd here and may be corrupt (perhaps for 'deploratione' or similar); rendered 'ruin'. Section 38: 'ab humana die' echoes 1 Cor. 4:3 ('human day', i.e. human judgment), rendered 'human court'. Scripture references printed in the edition are kept as given, corrected where the scan garbled them (Joel 2:12-13 for 'Joel 11, 22, 25'; Rom. 2:5-6; Jon. 3:5 for 'Joan. m, 5').

55: 'tectos' read as 'textos/contextos' (woven together). 57: 'Belus' read as 'fletus', 'succossit' as 'successit'. 46: 'nectua' read as 'noctua' (owl). 48: 'deductus sum' is masculine, as in the psalm quoted, though the speaker is the virgin. Several scriptural references in the edition are inaccurate (e.g. the Job citation in 46, Ps. 118:81 for 'your counsel is with you' in 51); they are rendered as printed or lightly corrected where the misprint is evident (Ps. 87:11 for 'LXXIVII').

nodes.text: THE ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE FALL OF A CONSECRATED VIRGIN.
CHAPTER ONE.

The author breaks his silence and rouses everyone to share the grief of the Church, which mourns because of the corruption of a sacred virgin; and having set out the shamefulness of the outrage, he utters his own sorrow over this matter.

1. Why are you silent, my soul? Why do you seethe with thoughts? Why do you not burst out into speech and lay bare the burning of your mind, so as to take some comfort? This plainly, this will be a kind of remedy for your sickness, if with open mouth you discharge the crime you have taken in. For an ulcer too, however swollen, once it has been opened, gives relief from the suffering as it lets off its heat.

2. Hear me now, you who are near and you who are far off, and you who fear the Lord, and rejoice together in the joy of his Church and mourn together in her sadness; as it is written: To rejoice with those who rejoice, and to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15). You, I say, I call upon, who hold fast the truest love of Christ, and do not rejoice over iniquity, but rather groan. Attend to the words of my mouth, and judge those things which proceed from just grief; and shudder together with me at the nature of the crime that has been uncovered.

3. A virgin of noble birth, dedicated to Christ, wise, learned, has fallen into the pit of disgrace; she has conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity: she has destroyed herself and stained the Church. From this every Christian soul has received a heavy wound; for what is holy has been given to dogs, and pearls have been cast before swine (Matt. 7:6): for by raging men the name of holiness has been torn apart, and by the unclean and filthy the precious resolve of chastity has been trampled underfoot.

4. Hence the seething in my soul, hence the incurable grief; for one evil drags many goods along with it, and the little cloud of one sinful woman has almost darkened the whole light of the Church. I will therefore take up the prophet's voice and say with weeping: Hear me, all you peoples, and see my grief: my virgins and my young men have gone into captivity (Lam. 1:12, 18). Truly this is captivity, where souls are led captive by sin to death and are possessed by the devil's dominion.
CHAPTER II.
He addresses the corrupted woman, and sets before her eyes what she was and how blessed before she committed the crime, and into what calamity and disgrace she afterwards fell.

5. To you, then, let my speech now be directed, who are the head and cause of these evils, who, wretched in many ways, have lost even the name together with the glory of virginity; for it is wrong for one who is not chaste to be called Susanna, and it is not permitted to be named a lily, which you are not. Where shall I begin? What shall I say first, what last? Shall I recall the good things you have lost, or lament the evils you have found?

6. You were a virgin in the paradise of God, indeed among the flowers of the Church; you were the bride of Christ, you were the temple of God, you were the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. And as often as I say 'you were', so often you must groan; for you are not what you were. You walked in the Church like that dove of which it is written: The wings of the dove covered with silver, and the hinder parts of her back in the appearance of gold (Ps. 67:14). You shone like silver, you gleamed like gold, when you went forth with a pure conscience. You were like a star shining in the hand of the Lord; you feared no wind, no clouds of war.

7. What is this sudden turning? What is this abrupt change? From a virgin of God you have become a corruption of Satan, from a bride of Christ a cursed harlot, from a temple of God a shrine of uncleanness, from a dwelling of the Holy Spirit a hovel of the devil. You who walked with confidence like a dove now lurk in darkness like a lizard. You who gleamed like gold because of the honour of virginity have now become baser than the mud of the streets, so that you are trampled even by the feet of the unworthy. You who had been a star shining in the hand of the Lord, as though falling from high heaven, your light has been put out and you have been turned into a cinder.
CHAPTER III.
How wretched she is, who now has no access to God, nor indeed even to men themselves: from which is understood the greatness of the shame she will one day suffer before the saints and angels.

8. Woe to you, wretched woman, and again woe, who have lost such great goods for the sake of a short time's lust! What hope have you left yourself with Christ the Lord, whose members you have taken and made the members of a harlot (1 Cor. 6:15)? Why will the Holy Spirit visit you, when you have repudiated him, who keeps himself far even from filthy thoughts?

9. But let us come to human things, so that through them divine things may be known. Look and see which of the holy men, or which of the holy women, does not shrink from coming near you: open your eyes, if you can; lift your brow, if you dare: look confidently at any one of the saints. Does not the consciousness of what you have done bow and weigh down your face like lead? Will not darkness and dreadful gloom hover before your eyes? Will not fear and trembling shake your soul and limbs?

10. If, then, buried in such heavy shame, you cannot look at men still in the flesh and liable to some fault, what will you do before the chaste apostles? What will you do before Elijah, Daniel, and so great an army of prophets? What will you do before John? What will you do before Mary, Thecla and Agnes, and the spotless choir of purity? What, finally, before the holy angels? Will you not be burned up, struck as if by lightning by the splendour and brightness of the spotless?
CHAPTER IV.

Having refuted the excuses which corrupted women usually put forward, he returns to the crime and pities the lot of her parents and of the whole household; he shows that it would have been more desirable for them that she had died first; and that no other comfort remains to them than that they consented, with the sole hope of divine reward, when she chose the profession of virginity; but that she has mocked their very expectation.

11. But perhaps you will say: I could not hold out, because I carried about fragile flesh. Blessed Thecla will answer you, with her countless companions: We too were clothed in the same flesh, and yet neither could the frailty of the flesh mutilate the full resolve of our chastity, nor could the savagery of tyrants cast it down through various torments. Truly, the flesh cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted. The guilt will therefore remain with the soul, which goes ahead of the flesh in pleasure.

12. But you will say: I did not want this evil; I suffered violence. That most courageous Susanna will answer you, whose name you falsely bear: I, placed between two elders, indeed between two judges of the people, set alone among the trees of the garden (Dan. 13:20 ff.), could not be overcome, because I did not want to be. How could you suffer force from one most foolish youth, and in the middle of the city, unless because you willingly wished to be defiled? Who, after all, heard your cries? Who perceived your struggling? But to pass over these things, certainly after the violence was inflicted you ought to have disclosed the crime, if not to others, at least to your parents or your sisters; for it would have been an excuse for your misfortune, it would have been a full cleansing of your conscience, if you had brought the enemy of your chastity out into public.

13. But perhaps you blushed, lest many should know you had been violated. And why did you fear where there was nothing to fear, unless so that by keeping silent about the crime you might more often be joined with the adulterer? Suppose, though, that shame prevented you from confessing: what do you say about the second union, what about the third, what about the frequent traffic of foulness? Let it cease, let the fiction of violence cease now, let the plea of shame cease, when so many times you offered those members dedicated to Christ to a most wicked adulterer, to be polluted by his body.

14. My soul shudders, shudders, my mind melts away, when it comes to the threshold of the crime. For a physician too, however strong in spirit he may be, when he cuts more deeply into a wound, will, I think, feel horror in some part. Alas, lost woman, do you now understand that all the ways of excuse are entirely closed to you? Do you now feel how much evil wicked lust has brought you both in flesh and in soul? 15. Your father had not expected this disgrace from you, he who counted you his singular glory. Your mother had not believed that this mourning and these tears would be born to her from you, she who consoled the groaning of her childbirth through your virginity. Your brothers, your sisters did not expect this dishonour from you, all of whom you have gravely wounded as if with the single sword of your crime.

16. If you had died by the common lot, your parents would have wept for you a little out of longing; but they would have rejoiced greatly, because they had sent ahead a spotless virgin, a living sacrifice to the Lord, an atoner, that is, for sins. But now they lament one dead and not dead; they mourn one living and not living: dead indeed to the glory of virginity, living in the dishonour of disgrace.

17. Your father is angry with his own body, from which you were begotten; your mother curses her womb, from which you unhappily came forth into this light. Yet they find no limit to their grief, except that they clearly seem to have this one comfort, that neither did your father compel you nor your mother force you to profess virginity, which you professed willingly and of your own choice. For I know that when your father set many difficulties before you, when he pressed upon you that the road of keeping virginity was arduous, you not only resisted stubbornly, but even said that terrifying revelations had been given to you.

18. So, as much as they hoped for a reward for themselves from not having opposed your resolve, so much, understand, wretched woman, does the weight of judgement grow against you; because you did not keep what you freely promised. With what coils has that most wicked serpent bound you? With what poisons has he infected you, he who deceived Eve, so as to strike you with such blindness, to cause such forgetfulness in your soul?
CHAPTER V.

He recalls to her memory on what day, with what rite, and with what concourse of people she was consecrated, adding that she ought rather to have shed her blood than violate her faith; and this he heightens by comparison with worldly marriages. Then he answers an objection drawn from the words of the Apostle.

19. Do you not remember the day of the holy resurrection of the Lord, on which you offered yourself at the divine altar to be veiled? In so great and so solemn an assembly of the Church of God, amid the shining lights of the newly baptised, amid the candidates for the heavenly kingdom, you had come forward as one about to marry the King. Do you not remember what address was made to you on that day: Look, daughter, behold, virgin, and forget your people and your father's house, and the King will desire your beauty; for he himself is the Lord your God (Ps. 44:11-12)? Remember, then, how great a people gathered for the wedding of your Bridegroom and Lord. You ought to have kept the faith which you promised before so many witnesses, always to have considered to whom you pledged your virginity. You ought more readily to have poured out your blood with your breath than to lose your chastity.

20. When these things had been said then, on that day of your consecration, and many praises of your chastity, you were covered with the sacred veil; there all the people, signing your dowry not with ink but with the spirit, cried out together, Amen. I am overcome by tears when I recall these things; I am pierced with goads when I consider these human examples. For if, when a betrothal has been made before ten witnesses and the marriage consummated, any woman joined to a mortal husband commits adultery not without great peril, what of when a spiritual union, made before the countless witnesses of the Church, in the presence of the angels and the hosts of heaven, is dissolved by adultery? I do not know whether a fitting death or punishment can be devised for her.

21. Someone will say: It is better to marry than to burn (1 Cor. 7:9). This saying applies to one who has not promised, to one not yet veiled. But she who has pledged herself to Christ and received the holy veil is already married, is already joined to an immortal husband. And now if she wishes to marry by the common law of wedlock, she commits adultery, she becomes a handmaid of death. If this is so, what must be said of her who is defiled by hidden and stealthy disgrace, and pretends to be what she is not? A virgin in dress, not a virgin in deed: twice an adulteress, both in act and in appearance.
CHAPTER VI.

He goes on to recall the things by which she ought to have been deterred from disgrace. And since she had already laboured under an evil reputation three years before, he marvels at her madness, in that, scorning alike enemies, friends and God himself, she broke through every barrier.

22. But I return to you again, who, having let so many good things fall into forgetfulness, have become a receptacle of so many evils. How did there not come into your mind, in that shameful act, your virginal dress, your procession into the church among the choirs of virgins? How did the light of the vigils not dazzle your eyes, the singing of the spiritual hymns not pierce your ears, the power of the heavenly readings not stir your mind, with the Apostle above all crying out to you from them: Flee fornication; for every sin whatever a man commits is outside the body, but he who commits fornication sins against his own body (1 Cor. 6:18)? And though he says: Against his own body, he nevertheless shows that he sins against Christ. For he adds: Or do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, which you have from the Lord, and that you are not your own? For you have been bought with a great price; glorify and carry God in your body (ibid. 19-20). And again he says: But let fornication and all uncleanness not even be named among you, as befits saints (Eph. 5:3). And setting aside all flattery, the Apostle fixes his sentence: Know this, he says, understanding that no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person will be an heir in the kingdom of Christ and of God (ibid. 5).

23. Did these things, so great and so terrible, not come into your mind when your members were sought for that wicked work? But a deadly forgetfulness was plunging you as into a very deep whirlpool, and accursed lust was leading you as a captive.

24. Ought you not at least to have remembered that place partitioned off with boards, where you stood in the church, to which devout and noble matrons used to run eagerly, seeking your kisses, women who were holier and worthier than you? Ought you not at least to have remembered those precepts which the inscribed wall itself pressed upon your eyes: The married woman and the virgin are divided: she who is not married thinks of the things of the Lord, how she may be holy in body and in spirit (1 Cor. 7:34). But you turned the saying to the contrary, so thinking and so acting that you were holy neither in body nor in spirit: in body, by fornicating; in spirit, by falsely claiming virginity.

25. Oh, the outrage! Report usually follows the deed; but in your case report ran ahead of the evil. For when, three years ago, there was a certain rumour and whispering about you, you pretended innocence and publicly demanded punishment of the slanderers in the church. What agitation I endured! What labours your father endured for your reputation, questioning everyone one by one, pressing everyone one by one, so that we might reach the author of the slander! For it was grievous to us, and intolerable to all good people, that anything shameful should be either said or believed about a virgin of God.

26. Nor did you fear this, nor keep it before your eyes, lest you become a joy to your enemies and make hostile those who laboured for your reputation. Very bold, very reckless, that your conscience did not frighten you; but with feigned virginity you thought you could deceive even God. But he who said: Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed (Matt. 10:26); and, You, he says, have acted in secret, but I will act in the open (2 Kgs 12:12); he who does not lie has brought the stealthy crime into public, and in the sight of this sun has laid bare the works of your darkness.

27. Oh, however far my speech extends, crueller things come to meet it; and wishing to restrain itself, it finds no limit. You forgot your resolve, forgot your parents, forgot the whole Church, forgot the glory of virginity, forgot the honour of your dignity, forgot even the promise of the kingdom, forgot the terrible judgement: you embraced corruption, you brought forth the fruit of shame, and as its end a most savage death and everlasting ruin.
CHAPTER VII.

He affirms that he gave her every care belonging to the episcopal office, but that she not only profited nothing from it, but even put a grave stumbling-block before others, which the Gospel shows to be condemned with the severest punishment.

28. And surely you have nothing to complain of in our negligence; for whatever belongs to the office of a shepherd was not denied either to you or to anyone. Spiritual love was applied, holy admonition was not lacking. Forgetting your father's house, as it is written (Ps. 44:11), you passed into a monastery of virgins. Placed among so many, I say not only that you ought to have been safe, if you had wished, but you could even have provided safekeeping for others. But in vain were these and other things provided.

29. In vain did I set forth the hymn of virginity, by which you might sing both the glory of your resolve and its observance alike. I sowed by the wayside, I sowed among thorns, I sowed on stony ground; for either the birds (Luke 8:5 ff.), that is, the demons, snatched my words from your heart, or they were choked by your evil thoughts, or they withered in the excessive heat of lust. Woe is me, for where I thought I was building gold, silver, precious stones, I am found to have laboured on wood, hay, stubble, materials to be burned (1 Cor. 3:12)! I too will say, with the prophet: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest (Mic. 7:1)!

30. And indeed, if you had done harm to yourself alone, there would be sorrow, but perhaps bearable. But now, how many souls you have wounded by your crime, how many souls you have made to repent of their resolve because of you! How many lips even of the faithful have been defiled by blaspheming the way of the Lord! The heathen have opened their mouth against us; the synagogue of the Jews has exulted against the holy Church through your disgrace.

31. But if he who causes one to stumble ought to be thrown into the sea with a millstone tied around him (Matt. 18:6), what do you pronounce of yourself, through whose crime every soul has been wounded, and the name of the Lord blasphemed among the nations? Is it not so that every time it is said, O virgins, so often the heap of your iniquity is increased? See, you lie wounded; see, you lie prostrate.
CHAPTER VIII.

What the difficulty and the method of the remedy he wishes to apply are: he urges her to take refuge not in just any penance, but in a fitting one, whose inward working, as well as its outward signs, is described here. Further, by its benefit she will obtain exemption from eternal punishment, provided she is the more severe on herself the less freely she confessed her sin. To this he also spurs her on by the terror of the judgment to come.

32. I want to help, but I cannot bring relief, because the whole head is in pain and the whole heart in grief: from the feet to the head, as Isaiah says, there is no place to put a poultice (Isa. 1:5, 6). Your sickness has shut out every aid of human medicine. And though both good and bad, moved by just indignation, judge you worthy of every ruin, judge that you should be tormented with every kind of torture, punished with death, or burned with fire, yet I, who know that heavier torments are kept for the wicked, and that tortures await impious souls without end, not temporal ones indeed but eternal, want you to be afflicted with other torments, ones that will certainly do you good and not destroy your soul.

33. So I will give counsel according to the divine sentence; for the one and only remedy to be tried is that which the divine voice holds out to the wretched through Ezekiel: I do not desire, it says, the death of the sinner, so much as that he should turn and live (Ezek. 33:11). And again: After this, says the Lord, I said: Turn to me. Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not come up (Jer. 8:22)? These sayings certainly savour of penance; these sentences of God call sinners to penance; for repentance is necessary for the fallen, just as medicines are necessary for the wounded.

34. But how great, and of what kind, do you think the penance must be? One that either equals the crimes or indeed exceeds them. See then whether this sin is simply adultery, or double, on account of that killing which is said to have been done in secret; and the greatness of the penance must be shown in proportion to the weight on the conscience. Penance, then, is to be performed not in words but also in deed. And it is performed thus: if you set before your eyes from what great glory you have fallen, and from what book of life your name has been erased; and if you believe yourself now placed close to the outer darkness itself, where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth without end. When you have grasped this in your mind with sure faith, as it truly is, that the soul which has transgressed must be handed over to the punishments of Tartarus and the fires of Gehenna, and that no other remedy has been established after the one baptism than the comfort of penance, be content to undergo however great an affliction, however great a toil, provided you are freed from the eternal punishments.

35. So, pondering these things with yourself and turning them over in your mind, be yourself a harsher judge of your deed. First of all, every care for this life must be killed off in you, and, regarding yourself as dead, as indeed you are, consider how you can come back to life. Next you must put on mourning clothes, and punish your mind and each of your limbs with fitting chastisement. Let the hair be cut off which through vainglory gave occasion for wantonness. Let the eyes stream with tears which looked on a man not innocently. Let the face grow pale which once blushed shamelessly. Finally, let the whole body be wasted with ill-treatment and fasting; sprinkled with ash and covered with sackcloth, let it shudder, since it took wicked pleasure in its beauty. And let the heart be melting like wax, troubling itself with fasting, and sifting in its thoughts why it was overthrown by the enemy. Let the mind too be tormented, because, though it had dominion over the members of the body, it yielded to an evil command.

36. Such a life, such a practice of penance, if it is persevering, will dare to hope, if not for glory, at least for release from punishment; for God says: Turn to me, and I will turn to you. Turn with your whole heart, in fasting, and in weeping, and in mourning; rend your hearts and not your garments; for he is kind and merciful (Joel 2:12, 13). Thus the great David, having turned, was justified; thus Nineveh, that sinful city, escaped the destruction hanging over it (2 Sam. 12:13). If, then, the sinner does not spare himself, he will be spared by God (Jon. 3:5 ff.). And if in this short span of life he makes up for the everlasting punishments of Gehenna to come, he will free himself from the eternal judgment.

37. A great wound needs deep and prolonged medicine: a great crime requires great satisfaction. For there is no doubt that the crime is lighter where a man confesses his sin of his own accord and repents; but where he hides his wrongs, is uncovered against his will, and is made public unwillingly, that is the graver crime. And you certainly cannot deny that this is what happened to you. And therefore you must grieve the more strongly, because you sinned the more strongly.

38. If sinful men saw in their minds what judgment God will send forth upon the world, and if the human mind were not scattered by worldly vanity nor weighed down by unbelief, they would most gladly endure for the present any torment, however great and of whatever kind, even if life were longer, provided they did not incur those punishments of eternal fire. But you, who have already entered the contest of penance, press on, wretched woman: cling to it strongly, as to a plank in a shipwreck, hoping to be freed through it from the depths of your crimes. Cling to penance to the very end of life, and do not presume that pardon will be given you by a human court, for whoever would promise you this deceives you. For since you sinned properly against the Lord, it is fitting that you await the remedy from him alone on the day of judgment.
CHAPTER IX.

He rebukes the seducer of the virgin, and terrifies him with the example of Belshazzar. He then warns him not to be content with inward torment but to embrace lawful penance; finally, so that he may not flatter himself on the great number of sinners, he reminds him of the burning of Sodom and the other cities, and urges him to break the snares of the enemy.

39. But what shall I say of you, son of the serpent, servant of the devil, violator of the temple of God, who in one wicked act committed two crimes, namely adultery and sacrilege? Sacrilege plainly, since with mad rashness you defiled a vessel offered to Christ and dedicated to the Lord. Belshazzar, that king of the Persians, who presumed to drink with his friends and concubines from the vessels of the Lord which his father had carried off from the temple at Jerusalem, was struck that same night by the hand of an angel and punished with a cruel death (Dan. 5:30): what do you think of yourself, lost and destroyer alike, who impiously violated and sacrilegiously defiled a rational vessel consecrated to Christ, sanctified to the Holy Spirit, forgetful of your own resolve and contemptuous of divine judgment? It would have been far better for you not to have been born at all than to have been born such that Gehenna should claim you as its own son.

40. And though the very consciousness of your crime drives you headlong in all directions (for the wicked flee when no one pursues them (Prov. 28:1)), though dreadful images of the sin terrify you not only awake but also asleep, yet, so that no medicine may be denied by the shepherd to a sick or dying sheep, I give counsel. Seek of your own accord the prison of penance; bind your inmost parts with chains; torment your soul with groans and fasts; seek the help of the saints; lie beneath the feet of the elect; so that your impenitent heart may not store up wrath for you on the day of wrath and of the just judgment of God, who will repay each according to his works (Rom. 2:5, 6). And do not place yourself among the number of those whom Paul mourns: Who sinned before, and have not done penance for the impurity and fornication and lusts they had committed (2 Cor. 12:21).

41. Nor flatter yourself on the multitude of those who sin in the same way, and say: I am not the only one who has done this, I have many companions; but reflect that a multitude of companions does not make crimes go unpunished. For in Sodom and Gomorrah and in all five cities countless peoples certainly lived, and all alike who used their bodies lustfully were burned up by showers of fire (Gen. 19:25); but Lot alone escaped from that inescapable burning (ibid. 29), because he had kept himself apart from that foulness.

42. So shut out, even now, unhappy man, the blandishments of the serpent from your heart, and with mourning and continual weeping, while that darkened soul dwells in your unclean body, acquire for yourself a remedy for the day of need, always having before your eyes the Apostle's sentence: For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10).
CHAPTER X.
Returning at last to the fallen virgin, he supplies her with certain stirring prayers and various feelings of penance, woven together from the Scriptures here and there.

43. Who will console you, virgin daughter of Zion? For your ruin has become as great as the sea. Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord (Lam. 2:13, 19); lift up your hands to him for a remedy for your sins. Take up, then, a lament. And first, let the fiftieth psalm not be left out on any day, for it was sung over such a matter; and run through it with tears and groaning as far as that verse: A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise (Ps. 50:19).

44. Besides this, pour out this lamentation also, not without compunction of heart, in the sight of God the judge: Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes (Jer. 9:1), that I may weep for the wounds of my soul? My feast days have been turned into mourning, and my songs into lamentation (Amos 8:10); the sound of hymns has departed, and the joy of psalms, and in their place has come gnashing of teeth and weeping of eyes. I was struck dumb and humbled, and kept silent even from good things, and my sorrow was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze up. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me (Ps. 38:3, 4). The abyss surrounded me, and at last sank my head into the clefts of the mountains (Jon. 2:6).

45. Alas for me, for I have become like Sodom, and been burned up like Gomorrah (Gen. 19:24); who will take pity on my ashes? I have offended more grievously than Sodom, for she had sinned without knowing the law, but I sinned against the Lord after receiving grace. If a man sins against a man, there will be someone to intercede; I have sinned against the Lord: whom shall I find to plead for me (1 Sam. 2:25)? I conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity; I opened a pit and dug it out, and fell into the ditch that I made. Therefore my sorrow has turned back upon my head, and my iniquity has come down upon my crown. My uncleanness is before my feet; I was not mindful of the last things, and I fell miserably (Ps. 7:15 ff.).

46. There is no one to console me. O how bitter is the fruit of wantonness! More bitter than gall, crueller than the sword. How have I come to desolation? Suddenly I failed, I perished because of my iniquity, like one rising from sleep; therefore in the city of the Lord my image has been brought to nothing (Ps. 72:19, 20). My name has been blotted out of the book of life; I have become like an owl in a dwelling, like a lone sparrow on a building: there is no one to console me. I look to the right, and I see that there is no one who knows me (Ps. 101:7 ff.). Flight has failed me, and there is no one who seeks after my soul (Ps. 141:5). I have become like a lost vessel; I have heard the reproach of all who live around me. Woe to that day on which my mother bore me, unhappy one, and this cruel light received me! It would have been better for me not to have been born than to become such a byword among the nations (Ps. 30:13, 14). Because of me shame has come upon all the servants of the Lord and those who worship him worthily (Job 3:3).

47. Mourn for me, mountains and hills; mourn for me, springs and rivers; for I am a daughter of weeping. Mourn for me, beasts of the forests, creeping things of the earth, and birds of the sky, and every soul that enjoys life. For you are blessed, wild beasts and birds, who have no fear of the underworld, nor must you give an account after death; for us there awaits the cruel punishment of Tartarus, because we sin though we have understanding; therefore there is no peace for sinners.

48. My sin, my iniquity, is not like the offences of men, for it is impiety. Having promised to keep my flesh virgin, and having publicly professed chastity, I lied to the Lord; therefore I have no confidence to call upon the Lord most high, for the mouth of those who sin has been stopped. For the Prophet sang of my evil, that those who withdraw themselves from God will perish: he destroys everyone who goes whoring away from him (Ps. 72:27). And again: My tongue has stuck to my jaws, and I have been brought down into the dust of death (Ps. 21:16).

49. Nevertheless I will cry to the Lord while there is still time, while space is given, for in death there is no remembrance, and in the underworld there is no confession: Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury. For your arrows are fixed in me, and there is no health in my flesh because of the face of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins. For my iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed down upon me. My scars have festered and grown worse because of the face of my folly. I have been afflicted with miseries and bowed down to the end; I roar from the groaning of my heart (Ps. 37:1-9). My heart is troubled within me, my strength has left me, and the light of my eyes is not with me (Ps. 37). O God, you have cast me off and destroyed me, you have shown me hard things, you have given me the wine of compunction to drink (Ps. 59:4, 5); I have been driven from your eyes, I shall no longer rise again to your holy temple, and I have come to ruin.

50. What profit is there in your blood, while I have gone down into corruption (Ps. 29:10)? Will you work wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up (Ps. 87:11)? It is your word, it is your promise: I do not want the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live (Ezek. 33:11). To you, my God, is my turning, for you alone can renew all things, and you call souls back from the underworld. You set the fettered free; you, O God, raise up those who are dashed down, give light to the blind, raise the dead.

51. I have gone astray like a lost sheep (Ps. 118:176): seek your handmaid, lest the cruel wolf swallow me. Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for her in her God (Ps. 3:3). But your counsel is with you (Ps. 118:81). How many are the days of your handmaid? When will you execute judgment for me? But do not enter into judgment with your handmaid (Ps. 142:2). My soul has fainted for your salvation, my eyes have failed in tears, my glory has been poured out on the ground (Ps. 118:81). When will you look upon me and restore my soul (Ps. 34:17)? For my iniquity you have chastised me, and made my soul waste away like a spider (Ps. 38:12). Remember, Lord, that I am dust: see my humiliation and my toil, and forgive all my sins (Ps. 24:18). Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and am no more, for in the underworld there will be no confession (Ps. 38:14).

52. You are able, Lord, to tear open my sackcloth and gird me with gladness (Ps. 29:12), to break my chains, by which I am bound and constrained, you who did not spurn filthy Rahab (Josh. 6:17). Take your anger from me, Lord, for I have sinned against you cruelly, until you justify my cause and lead me out into the light. God of hosts, grant my penance its effect and my confession perseverance, lest the deceiver of the soul harden me. I long, O God, for this gift, this grace, to be granted me from your fountain: that I may confess to you for ever, you who live and reign in the Trinity for ages of ages. Amen.
